title: A cello by Jean-Baptiste Vuillaume, Paris, 1862
description: labelled Jean Baptiste Vuillaume à Paris, 3 rue Demours Ternes. JBV., numbered 2420 and branded Vuillaume internally, and signed and dated in the upper treble bout of the back / length of back 29 13/16in., 75.8cm. / Sold with a copy of Agnès Briolle-Vieuxtemps' book Symphonie en Lac Majeur, Henry Vieuxtemps, L'âme du violin / Provenance / Henry Vieuxtemps (1820-1881) is one of the leading figures in the history of the violin in the 19th century. By the time he was nine, he had given his concert debut in Paris, and he became well known throughout Europe, Robert Schumann comparing him to Niccolo Paganini. He is well known for playing on two Guarneri del Gesù violins of circa 1741 (see Ingles & Hayday Notable Sales) but he also owned fine instruments by Stradivari and by his contemporary, Jean-Baptiste Vuillaume. Such was Vieuxtemps' celebrity that, at his funeral in Vervier in 1881, the funeral cortège packed the streets of the town, as his pupil Eugène Ysaÿe followed the hearse, carrying Vieuxtemps' beloved Guarneri violin. / Besides his formidable reputation on the concert platform, Vieuxtemps is best known today for his compositions, particularly his works for the violin, which include 7 concertos. However, he also wrote two cello concertos and a wide range of chamber music, including three string quartets. / In 1862 Vieuxtemps commissioned a quartet of instruments from his friend Jean-Baptiste Vuillaume. In 1863, after giving a tour of 53 concerts, of which several were quartet performances, he collected his new quartet in Paris, and later recalled the moment: "With my luthier friend, I shared all my thirst for sounds. He confided in me that he had understood Stradivari's secret regarding the varnish he used, I was amazed. Its sounds were indeed worthy of a Stradivarius. Vuillaume was an artist. A great artist. And he was the only one! I sent all my musician friends to his "luxury clinic" for exceptional instruments." / There was clearly a mutual admiration between the two men, as is reflected in a letter from Vuillaume to Vieuxtemps: "I cannot find words to express all the pleasure we felt yesterday admiring you as a violinist and as a composer. Admired is the word, and we are still delighted and spellbound by your magnificent talent." / Vieuxtemps' first string quartet was written some years after the acquisition of the instruments, which would no doubt have served as an inspiration to the composer; it is highly probable that Vieuxtemps performed his quartets on these instruments. / J.B. Vuillaume made a number of special quartets, named Count Doria (1848-63), Prince Caraman de Chimay (1865), Count Sheremetev (1865) and The Evangelists (1863). All of the quartets have subsequently been split up, with the exception of The Evangelists, which were sold by Ingles & Hayday in 2016. The cello from the Vieuxtemps quartet, however, is particularly noteworthy as it has remained in the possession of Henry Vieuxtemps' family for the 162 years since it was made, and is being offered for sale by his great-great grandchildren. / For more information about Vuillaume's quartets, please visit https://ingleshayday.com/features/the-evangelists-quartet-by-j-b-vuillaume/
